findings.mechanism: Replay should be scheduled as a curriculum: select highly prototypical/easy memories first, then gradually move toward less prototypical/harder memories, rather than uniformly replaying the buffer.
findings.quantitative_evidence: GRASP compared against 17 rehearsal policies and achieved higher continual-learning accuracy on ImageNet. Relative to uniform class-balanced replay, it reached the same performance with 40% fewer model updates; the paper also reports effectiveness on five text-classification datasets.
findings.evidence_scope: Online continual learning with replay buffers; ImageNet plus five text classification datasets. This supports replay ordering/selection efficiency, not a universal rule that easy-to-hard is optimal for every domain or agent memory.
findings.decision_relevance: Direct candidate for O's context/memory routing: retrieval order and rehearsal priority may matter as much as memory membership. A matched test could compare uniform/random retrieval against prototypical-first then progressively harder evidence while holding memory size and model calls fixed.

findings.mechanism: More replay is not monotonically safer: replay samples can geometrically conflict with task subspaces, so adding randomly selected past samples can increase rather than decrease forgetting.
findings.quantitative_evidence: The CoLLAs 2026 paper proves non-monotonic forgetting with replay in over-parameterized continual linear regression, constructs worst-case tasks where replay is harmful, and gives distributions where random replay increases forgetting in expectation. It also reports the effect with a neural network trained by SGD and on a standard benchmark.
findings.evidence_scope: Formal results are for linear-regression task-subspace settings; neural-network experiments show the phenomenon is not purely linear, but do not establish that replay is generally harmful.
findings.decision_relevance: Important guardrail for O's research-memory design: do not equate larger replay/context with better retention. Evaluate candidate memories by downstream interference and task relationship; this reinforces the existing Context Kernel principle that context has interference cost.

next_queries: Search accepted agent/LLM continual-learning papers for retrieval-order or replay-curriculum ablations analogous to GRASP.
Find methods that estimate task/memory compatibility before retrieval or replay and quantify interference reduction.
Search for active-data-selection methods that reduce model updates/cost under fixed retention targets.
Look for external-memory-only adaptation of LLM agents with frozen base weights and measured long-horizon transfer.

continuation.frontier: The strongest new thread is selective and ordered rehearsal, with explicit evidence that random/more replay can hurt. Next prioritize compatibility-aware retrieval/replay in LLM or autonomous-agent settings and cost-controlled ablations.
